The reply path drops the authoritative value — `accepted()` matches `Outcome::Accepted { .. }` (note the `..`) and discards `revision`, even though the protocol clearly carries it (the fixture replies `Outcome::Accepted { revision: 1 }`). So every retry recomputes `local + 1`, i.e. the *same* number after a rejection. If the coordinator's revision is ever ahead by more than one (an accepted `CandidateUpsert` refresh from the `refresh` path is the obvious source, and any duplicate/reordered command is another), `CancelCandidate{revision}` is rejected on every turn forever. Because that branch does `return Ok(true)` *above* the candidate-poll branch, one permanently-rejected candidate blocks polling and `Arm` for every other ready candidate — the original starvation, relocated from sealed releases onto new work. findings: [HIGH — liveness, fix is incomplete] `queue.rs::maintain` stale branch derives the new revision from local state only and never reconciles it: `SELECT ... json_extract(p.candidate_json,'$.revision')` feeds `revision.checked_add(1)`, and the incremented value is never written back to `candidate_json`. The reply path drops the authoritative value — `accepted()` matches `Outcome::Accepted { .. }` (note the `..`) and discards `revision`, even though the protocol clearly carries it (the fixture replies `Outcome::Accepted { revision: 1 }`). So every retry recomputes `local + 1`, i.e. the *same* number after a rejection. If the coordinator's revision is ever ahead by more than one (an accepted `CandidateUpsert` refresh from the `refresh` path is the obvious source, and any duplicate/reordered command is another), `CancelCandidate{revision}` is rejected on every turn forever. Because that branch does `return Ok(true)` *above* the candidate-poll branch, one permanently-rejected candidate blocks polling and `Arm` for every other ready candidate — the original starvation, relocated from sealed releases onto new work. Remedy: persist the coordinator-reported revision from the accept/reject outcome (or from the inspected grant's `candidate`) into `candidate_json` and cancel at `observed + 1`.

[MEDIUM — duplicate command amplification] The stale branch has no in-flight guard, unlike every sibling branch: the armed path writes `UPDATE attached_local_plans SET release_pending=1` before `seal_release`, `ready_release` is de-duplicated by `g.seal_json IS NULL`, and the poll path writes `SET poll_ms=?2` under `t.poll_ms<=?3`. The unarmed cancel path writes nothing, and its selection `ORDER BY t.ready_ms,p.rowid LIMIT 1` is deterministic over a row whose `ready_ms` does not change, so each `maintain` turn re-enqueues another `CancelCandidate` for the identical plan until a reply lands. The same function treats `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM attached_outbox` `>= 64` as hard backpressure — and that branch itself calls `pending(tx, Command::Acknowledge{..})` and returns, doing no other maintenance — so duplicate cancels consume the bounded outbox and can wedge releases and polling behind the overflow branch.

[MEDIUM-HIGH — resource accounting safety] `cleanup.rs::apply` hardcodes `user_code_released: false` for every ticket recovered from `attached_grants ... json_each(g.grant_json,'$.tickets')`. The only local evidence joined in is `attached_local_cleanup`, whose schema is `(invocation_id, boundary_sha256, proof_sha256)` — it does not carry the executor seal's `possibly_released` bit. This directly contradicts the model the accompanying barrier enforces: `wsl_maintenance.sql_barrier` raises unless `seal['possibly_released'] != (record['release_intent'] is not None)` is false, i.e. a journal record for an *issued* ticket must have `possibly_released == True`. Tickets listed in a grant snapshot are by definition issued, so the Rust path reports "never released" for exactly the population the Python barrier classifies as possibly released, under-reporting consumption of the shared debit to the coordinator. The comment "Its durable request and executor seal prove an unused obligation" is not backed by any stored field; thread `possibly_released` into `attached_local_cleanup` and use it, or refuse to synthesize cleanup for these rows.

[MEDIUM — contradictory derivation inside one transaction] `cleanup.rs::record_attached_cleanup` with `never = Some(..)` reads `ticket_json` from `attached_tickets`, writes `user_code_released: false` via `manager::release::record_unused_cleanup`, then unconditionally calls `apply(&tx)`. `apply`'s first loop selects `t.ticket_json,t.consumed ... WHERE t.cleanup_json IS NULL` and calls `manager::record_cleanup` with `user_code_released: consumed` — for that same ticket, in the same transaction, from the opposite source of truth. Nothing asserts `consumed = 0` when a `NeverReleased` proof is supplied, even though the row is already in hand; a `consumed = 1` ticket produces two mutually contradictory cleanup records. Add an explicit `InvalidState` check on `consumed` before calling `record_unused_cleanup`.

[MEDIUM — upgrade helper holds the store's write lock across daemon shutdown] In `upgrade-wsl-daemon.py::main`, `db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")` is followed by `executor_barrier(...)`, `save("barrier.json", ...)`, `subprocess.run(["systemctl","--user","stop","stillyard.service"], check=True, timeout=20)`, `poll.poll(5000)`, the link/replace, and only then `ROLLBACK` in the `finally`. The exclusive write transaction is therefore held for the entire stop plus exit wait (~25 s), so any SQLite write the daemon performs during clean shutdown blocks on the upgrader and either fails or times out the stop; the symptom surfaces only as the generic `RuntimeError("pinned old daemon did not exit")`. Related ordering point: the non-SQLite evidence (`cgroup.events`, `children`, journal `unsealed`) is captured *before* the stop, and the write lock fences the store, not the kernel or the journal file — so the emptiness proof recorded in `barrier.json` is up to 25 s stale at the moment of `os.replace`. Re-verify the journal/cgroup after the pidfd wait and immediately before replacement.

[MEDIUM-LOW — the one path that retains resources has no post-condition] `--allow-sealed-release-pending` is the only mode that swaps the binary while `leases.state='granted'` rows exist; `sql_barrier` returns `sealed_release_pending` with each `{lease_id, job_id, seals}` and it is persisted into `barrier.json`. Nothing after the restart checks that those lease ids actually reached `released`: the post-replacement loop only waits for `after["machine_scheduling"]["blocker"] is None` and then `save("after.json", after)`. Given the module's own contract ("only the daemon protocol may release its resources"), the helper should reopen the store read-only after reconnect and assert every retained `lease_id` is `released` with its grant sealed, failing loudly otherwise — otherwise a silently stuck release is indistinguishable from success in the evidence directory.

[LOW-MEDIUM — ineffective path containment in the barrier] `upgrade-wsl-daemon.py::executor_barrier` validates the cgroup path from the anchor with `if not executors.is_relative_to("/sys/fs/cgroup") or executors.is_symlink()`. `is_relative_to` is purely lexical and does not normalize `..`: `Path("/sys/fs/cgroup/../../tmp/fake").is_relative_to("/sys/fs/cgroup")` is `True` because `/sys/fs/cgroup` appears in `.parents`. Only the leaf is symlink-checked, so a symlinked intermediate component also passes, and `iterdir()`/`read_text()` then follow it. A mis-set or tampered `configuration.executor_cgroup` can point the emptiness proof at an ordinary directory holding a fabricated `cgroup.events` containing `populated 0`, defeating the barrier that the whole upgrade depends on. Use `resolve(strict=True)` plus a re-check, and confirm the filesystem is cgroup2.

[LOW — inconsistent identifier canonicalization, fails closed] `wsl_maintenance.sealed_pending_leases` builds `keys = {store_uuid + '~' + row[0] for row in invocations}` from raw DB text and compares that against journal keys, `attached_tickets.invocation_id` and `attached_local_cleanup.invocation_id`, while the containment comparison in the same loop normalizes (`record['containment'] != store_uuid + '~' + str(uuid.UUID(containment))`) and `sql_barrier`'s cleared loop normalizes invocations too (`store_uuid + '~' + str(uuid.UUID(invocation))`). Any formatting drift between the store and the journal makes the retained-lease path raise rather than compare, and a non-UUID invocation id is never rejected on this path. Normalize invocation ids once, at the top, in both functions.

[LOW — regression coverage does not cover the regression] The fixture exercises only an *accepted* cancellation: it asserts `revision == 2`, then `reply(&tx, &secret, Outcome::Accepted { revision })`, then `assert!(!queue::maintain(&tx).unwrap())`. The behaviour the fix exists for — a cancellation that is stale-rejected repeatedly — is never simulated, so nothing pins the retry semantics called out in finding 1; a change to `local + 1` would still pass. Two further gaps: after each `maintain` the fixture pulls a single `manager::pending` and never drains to `None`, so the doc comment's "At most one maintenance operation is added per turn" is unverified; and `test-wsl-maintenance.SealedPending` covers exactly one retained lease with only local-table mutations — there is no case with the two concurrently retained leases this recovery actually used, and no case with a journal record bound to a foreign lease (`records[key]['lease']` pointing at a second granted lease) exercising the `keys != journal_keys` check.
structured_output.summary: The ordering half of the fix is sound: hoisting the `ready_release` branch above the stale-candidate branch in `queue.rs::maintain` genuinely breaks the reported deadlock, and the fixture pins it (`Command::Release` before `CancelCandidate`, then `revision == 2`). The revision half is open-loop and incomplete: the cancel revision is derived from `candidate_json` which is never rewritten, and `accepted()` discards the coordinator's `revision` via `Outcome::Accepted { .. }`, so a rejected cancel is retried with the identical value forever — and because that branch returns above the poll branch, it starves arming of all other ready candidates. Two accounting flaws in `cleanup.rs`: the inventory-recovery branch hardcodes `user_code_released: false` for issued tickets using only boundary/proof digests, contradicting the `possibly_released` model the accompanying Python barrier enforces, and `record_attached_cleanup` can write two contradictory cleanups in one transaction because it never asserts `consumed = 0` alongside a `NeverReleased` proof. In the helper, the upgrade holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` across `systemctl stop` and the pidfd wait (shutdown-write deadlock risk, and cgroup/journal evidence stale by up to ~25 s at replacement), `is_relative_to(\"/sys/fs/cgroup\")` is lexical so `..` and symlinked intermediates pass, and the one mode that retains granted leases across the swap has no post-restart check that those lease ids actually reached `released`. Scoped to the recovery slice as requested; not an MR3 exit judgement.
